body:
my PG email showed this form:

```

INSERT INTO mytable (id, a, b)
SELECT nextval("mytable_id_seq"), p1, p2 FROM (
    SELECT p1, p2 FROM (VALUES (10, 11, 1), (12, 13, 2)) AS sel(p1, p2, num) ORDER BY num
) AS ss RETURNING mytable.id
```

which is still not what I have above.  VALUES supports ORDER BY following the VALUES () keywords though I dont know how this is supposed to look if we havent given the VALUES column names.

claude:

Yes, in the second statement (the direct one), the order in which nextval() is executed will match the order of the VALUES tuples as sorted by ORDER BY num.
INSERT INTO mytable (id, a, b)
SELECT nextval("mytable_id_seq"), p1, p2 FROM (VALUES (10, 11, 1), (12, 13, 2)) AS sel(p1, p2, num) 
ORDER BY num
RETURNING mytable.id
In this case:
The VALUES are sorted by num (so order is: (10, 11, 1) first, then (12, 13, 2))
The SELECT processes rows in that sorted order
nextval() is called for each row in that order
First nextval() call → row with p1=10, p2=11
Second nextval() call → row with p1=12, p2=13

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **main** branch:

**run sentinel server side fns outside of VALUES** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/6499

this issue is strictly PostgreSQL.  The whole logic we have in compiler for insertmanyvalues with a server side expression is only a PG thing right now.   SQL Server does not support batching in this mode, apparently (though maybe it's supposed to).
correction, sql server is in there, need to figure out what's what

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **rel_2_0** branch:

**run sentinel server side fns outside of VALUES** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/6500

the scope of this change is limited to just PostgreSQL and just within compile.py, it's a straightforward move of some columns and we have lots of tests for this, so I'm linking this to 2.0 and we can see how it goes.

> VALUES supports ORDER BY following the VALUES () keywords though I dont know how this is supposed to look if we havent given the VALUES column names.

you can use positions, so `ORDER BY 3`
also it seems that, at least on postgresql, you can use `columnN` as implicit names of the columns, so `VALUES (1,2,1), (2,3,1) ORDER BY column3` works
naming with AS should be equivalent
The order by is applied to the select though, not the values

i dont think it actually matters?

EXPLAIN shows it is doing column3:

```
test=> explain SELECT nextval('mytable_id_seq'), p1, p2 FROM (VALUES (10, 11, 1), (12, 13, 2)) AS sel(p1, p2, num) ORDER BY num;
                                QUERY PLAN                                
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Result  (cost=0.04..0.07 rows=2 width=20)
   ->  Sort  (cost=0.04..0.04 rows=2 width=12)
         Sort Key: "*VALUES*".column3
         ->  Values Scan on "*VALUES*"  (cost=0.00..0.03 rows=2 width=12)
(4 rows)

```

this would be a concern if the idea was it gets the rows from `(VALUES (10, 11, 1), (12, 13, 2)) AS sel(p1, p2, num)` in random order, the assembles all the randomly ordered rows w the nextval, then orders them.

hey.    there's  a way to test this.    in the code we can have it randomly scramble the tuples in the VALUES.   hee hee.   let's try that

> EXPLAIN shows it is doing column3:

indeed, explain show the same exact plan, so I guess it's equivalent

here's a local test

```
test=> SELECT nextval('mytable_id_seq'), p1, p2 FROM (VALUES (13, 14, 3), (10, 11, 1), (14, 15, 4), (12, 13, 2)) AS sel(p1, p2, num) ORDER BY num;
 nextval | p1 | p2 
---------+----+----
      11 | 10 | 11
      12 | 12 | 13
      13 | 13 | 14
      14 | 14 | 15
(4 rows)

```

im trying to see if i can inject this into the code, but i have to isolate it to only when we have this SQL form

so yeah you can do this:

```diff
diff --git a/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py b/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py
index 371d872b4..3fffcdf71 100644
--- a/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py
+++ b/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py
@@ -6012,6 +6012,10 @@ class SQLCompiler(Compiled):
                         {f"{key}__{i}": param[key] for key in keys_to_replace}
                     )
 
+                if imv.embed_values_counter:
+                    import random
+                    random.shuffle(replaced_values_clauses)
+
                 replaced_statement = statement.replace(
                     "__EXECMANY_TOKEN__",
                     ", ".join(replaced_values_clauses),

```

and *with the patch*, tests pass.  There are four tests that fail, and all four of those are variations that are putting the "sentinel" on a column other than the primary key, where the primary key itself has a Sequence on it; those tests still embed the nextval() in the values(), because in those tests the sequence is not the sentinel.

so i think we're good for PG for now.   MSSQL and MySQL, they are more difficult to test for these since they use positional params and I'd have to get the shuffles exactly right
